utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Stanisic and Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Simatovic, can you hear me in a language you understand? Apparently not. Mr. Simatovic, can you hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED SIMATOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You still can hear me in a language you understand. Yes, thank you. Could I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I am Dermot Groome, I am accompanied by Doris Brehmeier-Metz, Klaus Hoffmann, and we are assisted today by Thomas Laugel and Vickie Iacobellis. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. The Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, myself, Geert-Jan Knoops, and accompanied by legal assistants Amy Walsh, and Rima Dykstra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. The Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Zoran Jovanovic. And together with Mr. Domazet and Ms. Morgan, we are the Defence team for Frenki Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Knoops, the Chamber received a signed waiver form for this afternoon saying that Mr. Stanisic waives his right to be present. Yes. Nevertheless, we also received a report dated the 2nd of June concerning the health condition of Mr. Stanisic, and despite the fact that Mr. Stanisic has waived his right, the Chamber would like to receive some additional information on this report. And we have understood that Dr. Eekhof is stand-by, and that we could ask questions to him through a videolink. Is that correct, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then have the videolink activated. Yes. I -- yes. The videolink has been established. Is it -- Mr. Eekhof, Dr. Eekhof, at the other side of the line? You can hear me? You can see me?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can see you, and we can hear you, Dr. Eekhof. First I would like to ask the parties if I put questions to Dr. Eekhof in relation to the medical report, is there any need as far as the parties are concerned to ask him to make a solemn declaration or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, not from the Prosecution's point of view, but I'm unable to hear the remote location, so when the usher is able, I'd appreciate if she could check my electronic system here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam usher will assist you. Mr. Knoops, any need to ask Dr. Eekhof to make a solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic? No need for that. I have a few questions for you, Dr. Eekhof. We've received your report of the 2nd of June today in which you describe that you provide us with information. You first deal with the, as you said, presumed short period of unconsciousness. May I take it that you're not certain about whether there was any period of unconsciousness and that's why you used the word "presumed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, nobody was present, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Until proven otherwise, we always use the term "presumed." It does not mean I do not believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Then that is clear to me. The next line -- the next paragraph deals with the back pain. You say it's improving slowly. That means that Mr. Stanisic slowly is having less back pain?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, and he's getting more mobile slowly. He's more -- in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has he received any physiotherapy treatment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's been offered to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] And as far as I know, he's refused twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And on -- who indicated that this might be -- because we do not find anything in the neurological report that physiotherapy might improve his condition. Was that your assessment? Was that the assessment of the medical expert? Could you tell us what -- who indicated that this might be a proper treatment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, the neurologist could not find -- could not explain the complaints by neurological things. And as Mr. Stanisic had been lying for quite a long time, Dr. Falke had prescribed physiotherapy, to get active quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now is it to improve his mobility because he has been lying for quite a while --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or do you expect also any positive effect in relation to his back pain?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, he's been lying so long that he needs to get more active, and being more active would relieve the pain in the long run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I do understand that he has not received it because he doesn't want to receive such treatment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next line is clear to me, that is, colitis unchanged. The next line, psychological situation, unchanged. I'd like to move to your conclusions. First you say he's not fit to be transported. Could you explain to us on what this conclusion -- on what factors this is based?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mostly on the back pain. He's been transported to the hospital for the MRI and other exams by specialists, but it's always quite painful experience for him, which I do believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last words were "which I do believe." Is it a matter of belief or is it a matter of establishing on the basis of medical findings that he's suffering from this back pain?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, pain, as you know, can never be objective. We have to rely on what the patient says. Moving around, he does give a painful impression. And I heard when he went to the hospital, it was quite painful for him. And he complained at the moment and said it was possible for him to go see a specialist, so I assumed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now following your own words, you said when he went to the hospital it was quite painful for him, and he complained at the moment when it was -- so what you say he was complaining about pain. Whether it was painful or not, you conclude that on what the patient told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's what I have to -- what we have to rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Next conclusion that he's not fit to sit for more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain the basis for this conclusion and also explain the ten minutes' limit which you -- which we find in your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, trying to objectively look into it, we ask him to check what his daily routines are. And during the meals he sits down for ten minutes, but after that he goes back to bed, presumed because of his back pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the conclusion that he's not fit to sit more than minutes is therefore mainly deduced from what you observe what he is doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. Next is he is fit enough to participate in proceedings if sitting is limited to ten minutes. That is based on this same observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] On the same observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last of your conclusions is he's fit enough to participate in proceedings up to one hour in the bed that has been installed in the video teleconference room. Could you explain what led you to conclude that it was up to one hour that he would be fit to participate in proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, also this is based on observations. But when talking about his health and when visiting him, he can -- we can hold normal conversations or talked about half an hour. And the hour is always a guess, of course, we cannot base that on real objective facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I, at this moment, have no further questions, but I'm looking at my colleagues. Has any of the parties any questions to Dr. Eekhof? Yes, perhaps it would be in light of the circumstances, Mr. Knoops, to give you first an opportunity, if you have any further questions, and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Eekhof, could you just confirm whether you can see Mr. Knoops standing at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can see him. I can't see what you can see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Eekhof.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, in your report you refer to the unchanged psychological situation of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: What do you mean with the word "unchanged"? What is the level of reference in regard to this qualification?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It was the level when I first met him, so I'm writing weekly reports to the Trial Chamber and his psychological situation has not improved, clearly now that we write it clearly in this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Does the word "unchanged" refer to the findings of Dr. Petrovic of the 10th of May in a report?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, more or less. I read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Was the report you filed today substantiated by an additional report of Dr. Petrovic about the psychological situation of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] By that report, yes. I have not spoken to him today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So there is -- with respect to this report new report of Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Sorry, I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that there may be some confusion. I think Mr. Knoops was asking whether you took into account any new report compared to the one which was delivered on the 10th of May. Did you see any new report?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So, in fact, the qualification "unchanged" is based on the report of the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] And my own observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Observations, yeah. Dr. Eekhof, you also state in your report that in your opinion as a general practitioner, there are no evident psychiatric reasons preventing him from participating in proceedings. I can deduce from your answer just a few seconds ago that there wasn't a separate psychiatric evaluation --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: -- which underlie your reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: How far -- because you state that he is fit enough to participate in proceedings up to one hour in the bed that was installed in the VTC room. How far did you -- were you able to deduce from the level of depression of Mr. Stanisic whether he was able to participate in proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, as a GP we're trained to judge depressions. We're not psychiatrists, which means there was this possibility that we judge it a bit different. But I -- most of my conclusion is on the fact that normal conversations are necessary, and the list of things we check are unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to evaluate, for instance, the level of concentration, the level of active participation of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I judge it by -- with my conversations with Mr. Stanisic. He is fully aware and concentrated when we speak. That's what I base it. That's the basis of my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In the report of Dr. Petrovic also mentioned in your first medical report, it's mentioned that the psychological situation has worsened. It's a report of 12 May.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I know, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did anything develop in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, he has contacted Dr. Petrovic again. And as I understand [indiscernible] been organised. But since the 12th of May, the situation, in my opinion, has not changed much, not positive nor negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And was there any incentive to review the psychiatric situation of the accused after the 12th of May by an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] In my opinion, not, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would it be your advice to the Court to have the situation anew evaluated by an independent expert in the psychiatric field?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It might be a good idea, as, of course, I'm a GP and not a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour, at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. Mr. Jovanovic, may I take it that you have no questions for Dr. Eekhof?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any further questions on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome may have some questions for you, Mr. Eekhof.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, I'd like to focus your attention on the back pain that you describe in your report, and would you please address the issue of pain medication. Has there been any discussion or consideration of whether pain medication might ease Mr. Stanisic's discomfort and allow him to sit in a chair or lie in the bed for a longer period of time than mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] He is on some medication at the moment. Now, back pain can be very severe, even though it is not a serious ailment. I do not -- I think the combination of medication and the physiotherapist would help. He's luckily also been more active, walking around more often than he did a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm a little bit confused. Is he currently being prescribed medication to ease that back pain now?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is he complying with the taking of that medicine?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your assessment in terms of how long he is able to remain sedentary either in a chair or in a bed is based upon him maintaining the medicine that you've just -- you've already prescribed?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, since no one seems to have further questions to you, I would like to thank you very much for making yourself available, and you are accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can close the videolink. We're here today for a Pre-Trial Conference. It has been established that Mr. Stanisic has waived his right to be present, and we have heard more about his medical condition at this moment. The first item -- the first issue I'd like to raise is the time that is available for the Prosecution and the number of witnesses to be called during the Prosecution's case. The Chamber wonders whether the Prosecution could explain why the witness list of the 6th of May of this year was not in conformity with the Rule 73 bis (C) determination made by the Chamber at the Pre-Trial Conference on the 28th of April, 2008. At that occasion the Trial Chamber decided that the number of witnesses to be called would be limited to 90, and that the number of hours was set at a maximum of 130 hours. Now, the witness list of the 6th of May of this year includes 107 witnesses, and there is a pending application to add one witness to that list, so that would make the total number 107. And the time which is used for the examination of these witnesses is assessed at 183 and a half hours. Mr. Groome, any way why the decision of the Chamber of last year would not stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there was some confusion as to whether that would have been one of the decisions that the Chamber would consider afresh. If it is the Chamber's decision that the Prosecution is bound by that decision, then I would be bound by that decision, then I consider myself bound by that decision, and I would only ask to the end of the week to re-file the consolidated witness list to bring it in conformity or full conformity with Judge Robinson's determination made on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it comes a bit of surprise when other respects, clarification was sought on what exactly should be done again and not necessarily be again, that this rather important issue, that you did not seek any clarification at all, and that you just moved on as if the 53 and a half additional hours would be granted. It comes as a bit of a surprise. And apart from that, it takes quite a lot of work, isn't it, to do the job twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for that, Your Honour, but I assure you it wasn't any presumption on the Prosecution's part that we were going to get any time -- any additional time that the Chamber did not intend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we -- the Chamber will have to look at your new witness list to see whether there's any reason to change anything, but the Chamber expects you, first of all, to file a witness list and whatever other submissions you would like to make that you could even do with less than 130 hours of why you would, in view of this one additional list, why you might need 133 hours. I mean, the Chamber waits for any further submissions on the matter, but the starting point at this moment is that the ruling of last year --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be acceptable for us to file a new consolidated witness list by the end of the week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, until Friday -- you've got until Friday, close of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll also not at this moment further deal with the matter. We'll just wait and see what your new filing will bring us, unless any of the Defence counsel would like to make any comments or any submissions on the matter at this stage. I see from nodding no simultaneously by two Defence counsel that there's no need for that. Then I move on to the next item which is the modalities of trial. On the 29th of May of 2009, the Chamber issued its decision on the start of the trial and the modalities for trial, and I take it that the parties have read this decision by now. I'd like with to make one addition to item 1 of the modalities. Ideally with court hearings two days per week, for trial management purposes, it would be best to sit on Thursday and Friday one week, and then Monday and Tuesday the week after. But the Chamber aims not to sit on Fridays. Therefore, if the courtroom schedule allows, we'll aim to sit on Wednesday and Thursday, and then the week after that on Monday and Tuesday. Scheduling is a rather complex issue. Are there any questions in relation to the decision, the decision on the start of the trial and the modalities? I see you're on your feet, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one point of clarification. In paragraph 10 of the Trial Chamber's decision, the Chamber accepts the Prosecution's argument that there must be a bifurcation of any assessment of Mr. Stanisic's health when the medical treatment he receives by his care providers. The issue I wish to raise with the Chamber is the following. In paragraph 3 of the annex attached to that decision, the Chamber requires the UN Detention Unit reporting medical officer to submit a weekly report on the medical condition of the accused and a gastroenterologist once every four weeks. What is not clear to me, Your Honour, and I seek clarification from the Chamber, is whether the personnel that will be providing such reports will have any responsibility with respect to the treatment of Mr. Stanisic, or will they be completely independent assessors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear as a matter of clarification. Any questions by the other parties or any further submissions in relation to what was just raised by Mr. Groome. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sorry, not by Mr. Groome, another note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any other -- then we'll deal with them after we've heard all the questions. Mr. Knoops, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Defence for Mr. Stanisic would like to raise the content of paragraph 7 of the annex. Actually, we were hesitant to raise it today, but now that we heard the testimony of Dr. Eekhof we would like to suggest to the Chamber in order to assist the speediness of the trial to -- alongside the reporting by the medical officer of the UNDU also to have a weekly or two-weekly report of a psychiatrist, not being Dr. Petrovic -- or it could be Dr. Petrovic, for instance, by doctor De Man. The problem we might face in the future is that once the Court would follow the reasoning in paragraph 7 that on the day of the particular court session, the Court might face the necessity to invoke what it says an independent medical expert to familiarise herself with the medical situation of Mr. Stanisic. Now, what we have received until so far are updates by Dr. Eekhof on mainly the physical situation of the accused while he's referring to a report in this situation on 10th of May of Dr. Petrovic concerning the psychological condition. It might be of assistance to the Court to have alongside the reporting system as set out in paragraph 7 for that scenario, also beforehand a reporting system in place, for instance, by Dr. De Man on the psychiatric situation of the accused. Today we heard that, although Dr. Eekhof is as a general practitioner, familiar with some of the psychological aspects of the accused's health, he's not an expert on that. And I think the statement he gave today does give rise to certain questions as how can the psychological or psychiatric situation be assessed on the basis of a document of the 10th or the 11th of May? And by suggesting this to the Court, we could therefore prevent the situation we had last year, namely, that on the day of the particular court session the Court confronted with a statement from the medical officer has to assign or has to invoke a psychiatric expert to evaluate that component of the health of the accused. That could cause several delays when the Chamber would decide to go alongside that route. And, therefore, if the Chamber could consider to have such a system in place, an additional reporting system by a psychiatrist, that could maybe beforehand solve quite some delays. And we as Defence, we have, of course, several questions as to the -- the foundation of a statement of a general practitioner as saying, Well, his psychological situation has not been changed or his psychiatric situation has not changed. And still we might face the situation that the accused for mental reasons is not able to come to court or participate. And, therefore, it is a suggestion on the basis for experience of last year to the Court to consider this addition to paragraph 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me start in reverse order. Mr. Knoops, you have made a suggestion to expand the -- paragraph 7. The Chamber will consider your suggestion, we'll think about it, and you'll hear from the Chamber what the conclusion would be. Mr. Groome, if there's any need to make further submissions on the suggestions made by Mr. Knoops, then, of course, you have an opportunity, and I'll give you an opportunity to do that. But we'll not decide on the matter immediately. So the second issue, Mr. Groome, the -- whether or not the reporting doctors are involved in the treatment of Mr. Stanisic is a matter of constant concern by this Chamber. The fact that we are talking about a reporting medical officer is already the result from trying to clearly separate who treats and who reports. Now, unfortunately where it looked as if a reporting medical officer, a general practitioner, would not be involved in the treatment of Mr. Stanisic, it now turned out that Dr. Eekhof plays a role - perhaps not the most important role - in the treatment of Mr. Stanisic. Which, as it was phrased, I think is that he is now involved in the pathway of treatment, which, of course, interfered with what the Chamber had on its mind and what was discussed earlier with the parties about who reports and who treats. The Chamber is in an ongoing discussion with the Registrar, the UNDU, and medical experts in order to have a clear picture on who treats and who reports because the combination of the two might not be the best solution under the present circumstances. This may be not a very satisfactory answer to you apart from that the matter is under our attention every single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need -- would you like to respond to Mr. Knoops' suggestion, or would you prefer to do that in writing, but then, of course, not in two weeks, but if you want to think about I want --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I can respond very simply, and it's just to recall some of the points raised in the Prosecution's submission on the modalities is that the Prosecution also feels that it would be beneficial, having also learned from the experience last year to have this independent psychological assessment. So the Prosecution in some ways agrees with Mr. Knoops that there would be some benefit in having a person report to the Chamber, be assessing Mr. Stanisic on a regular basis, so we are not in the situation where it arises at the last moment, witnesses are in The Hague, and it's a rather difficult situation to deal with at that stage. So I do support Mr. Knoops' suggestion in part with respect to another independent assessing psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. The Chamber will, as I said, Mr. Knoops consider the matter and let you know. If there's nothing else in relation to this matter, I would like to move on to the next item which is trial scheduling during June and July. On the 6th of May, 2009, the Stanisic Defence requested for postponement of commencement of the trial. And on the 12th of May the Prosecution responded that it took no position with regard to the motion. During the Status Conference on the 12th of last month, the Chamber decided for a variety of reasons which were totally unrelated to the request by the Stanisic Defence to reschedule the Pre-Trial Conference from the 18th of May to today, the 2nd of June. On the 2nd of June -- on the 27th of May, the Chamber decided to deny the Stanisic Defence's request and informally communicated this decision to the parties through an e-mail from the Senior Legal Officer. The Chamber considered that even under the difficult organisational circumstances of the present case a Defence counsel need to prioritise its Tribunal obligations. Also, since the trial would not be starting full time, the Chamber considered that the parties would have time to conclude other professional obligations. The Chamber indicated that in the -- indicated in the already-mentioned informal communication that scheduling considerations anyway might prevent the opening statements being heard earlier than four weeks from the original as-planned date of the 25th of May, 2009. So the practical effect might not be any different from when we would have granted the request, but we have denied it, but it might not make that much of a difference. One of the things the Chamber in relation to this would like to ask to you, Mr. Knoops, whether you have any already-established court appearances on such days so that we could see to what extent we could take that into consideration. Of course, there's still co-counsel, Mr. Jordash, but of course we're aware not trying to make life any more difficult for you as it is already. Could you give us any set dates for court appearances which would make it difficult for you to appear in the Stanisic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honours, thank you very much for your patience with the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic and also the fact that you're willing to consider it and accommodate our problems. The main -- I can provide maybe that's more efficient for today provide tomorrow morning a list with some dates which are, for me, quite difficult to change. But on the other hand Mr. Jordash's main concern was his other obligation in the appeals case in Sierra Leone, the dead-line he had to meet this week. And our other obligation case relates to Michel Bagaragaza at the ICTR which is already postponed twice which makes it for us unsecure when this case could start. It's still unclear. But with respect to, say, some domestic court sessions which, for me, are very vital to attend, I could provide the Court tomorrow with a list tomorrow, but it will be a short list, I can promise. The Defence will do as much as possible to have either Mr. Jordash or myself in court, and I will get back to the Chamber as soon as possible with some dates in June or July, but there will be few of them. Our main problem was the month of May which is now covered by the other postponement by Your Honours' other reasons. If that may help the Court I can provide, as said, this list as soon as possible with the dates. For us, the main problem remains how the ICTR will schedule the Bagaragaza case. The last information is that it's being postponed until after the summer recess, and even then it's still not sure when the case will go to trial. We were informed that because of a lack of capacity of the Judges, the case which was originally scheduled for February and then April has now been pushed back until after summer recess. But we'll keep the Court informed about any court date of the ICTR in the Bagaragaza case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there would be any -- we do understand that this scheduling is uncertain at this moment. If in any of your domestic cases your appearance in domestic courts would possibly result in a non-representation of Mr. Stanisic, then of course we would like to have full details of whether it's trial, whether it's pre-trial, and where and -- so that we can see how we can -- whether and if so how we can accommodate the Defence. I already informed you that the Registry is currently working out a schedule for the beginning of this trial. This has not yet been finalised. As I said before, it's a complex matter. The Chamber will inform the parties as soon as possible when the opening statements in this case will be heard and when the presentation of evidence will commence. I already, however, can inform you that this Chamber will not sit in the Stanisic/Simatovic case in the week of the 22nd up to the 26th of June and that we will also not sit in the week following immediately the recess. The recess ends on the -- let me -- no, the formal recess is -- and I think they usually take it from the Monday to the Monday. But the last date in court before the recess is the 24th of July and the first day after the recess is the 17th of August, but this Chamber will not sit in that first week, that is, the week of the 17th up to and including 21st of August, which would mean that we would, at its earliest, restart at the 24th of August. Any further questions in relation to this matter? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on the matter of scheduling, if I could advise the Chamber, the Prosecution stands ready on very short notice to give its opening. The opening is prepared. I am advised that it may be difficult to bring witnesses here in less than two weeks' notice. Of course we will endeavour to do that should the Chamber schedule hearings. But with the requirement of visas and that, I am informed that it may be some with some difficulty that a witnesses brought here in shorter than a period of two weeks. So the Prosecution would appreciate as much advanced notice as possible as to when the Chamber would like to hear evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is aware of problems that sometimes arise from getting visa. Sometimes there's also a problem in getting passports. That, of course, can be dealt with at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have dealt with that. It's just the visa question that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the visa question. Any further matter in relation to scheduling? Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're discussing some technical problems which are obviously increasing and due to the timetable which we have to abide by. In such situations there is always communication between the Defence and the Registry and the Defence team for the accused Simatovic, that is, my learned colleague and myself are not residents in Holland as are the lawyers representing Mr. Stanisic, so that we have a constant problem in communicating with the Registry regarding the need to be present in The Hague and what the status of the time spent in The Hague is. Last year almost throughout the meetings it wasn't clear whether the case was in the pre-trial or trial status, and this went on until a few days ago when I communicated with the Chamber which is charging us membership fees as if we were in the trial stage though we are in the pre-trial stage. These are really minor issues, and I'm sorry for raising them before the Trial Chamber, but the Registry requires explanations why we're in The Hague, whether the time spent here can be counted as two weeks prior to trial, or is it longer than that? So there are series of formalities which we have to deal with and which encumber our activities regarding the case itself. I should also like to know if at all possible with greater precision when the trial is due to begin. I didn't quite understand whether you said we won't be working in the week from the 22nd to the 26th, whether the opening statement is due after the 26th or before the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, unfortunately, I can't answer that question at this moment. I have good expectations that the work on the schedule may be finalised within the next one or two days. And of course we'll immediately inform you about that. It is a matter of Judges sitting in various other cases. Sometimes again with other Judges while sitting in other cases. So it is a rather complex matter. We have to find courtrooms. Not always all courtrooms are fit to have all cases. Therefore, it is -- we expect to come up with a June and July schedule still this week. And unfortunately, I can't tell you anything more at this moment, but the -- one of the first things I did this morning is asked my staff whether we had already the schedule, because I'm fully aware what problems it may cause you. I hope that there will be more clarity within a couple of days. If there's anything about explanations requested by the Registry, the Registry knows that the Chamber - and I as a Presiding Judge of this Chamber am always available to give additional information and explanation and information on matters that bothers them - and I would not mind if there's any further problem, not to say that you are not in a position that you have to respond to their questions, but you may quote this line of the transcript if matters remain unresolved. This is not a promise that I can resolve every issue, but I will do my utmost best to see whether matters can be arranged in an acceptable way for all parties, the Chamber, and the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Moving on from the scheduling issue to the next item on my agenda, which is about list of documents to be used with witness testimony. The parties are encouraged to agree on how much time in advance the list of documents the parties intend to use during the examination of the witnesses should be provided to the other party and to the Chamber. In this respect the, especially in view of the cross-examining party's obligations, that is, when, at what specific moment to provide the party that has called the witness with the exhibits it intend to use, I'd like to -- the Chamber would like to draw the -- your attention to the extensive case law on this subject. And if you'd like to have an overview, the parties might, for example, consult a decision which was given in the case against Gotovina et al., a decision on the 5th of December, 2008. The Chamber received a copy -- a copy of a proposal for an agreement between the parties which was sent by the Prosecution to the Defence today. First of all, receiving this copy leads me to make two short comments. The first comment is that the Chamber does not want to get involved in ongoing negotiations. Sending a copy of a proposal may be understood as, Look how reasonable we are, and that's of course exactly what should not be dealt with in court. The Chamber should stay out of that unless there is a moment where the parties say, We've tried our best. We cannot reach an agreement. Could the Chamber either rule on the matter or could the Chamber further assist the parties in reaching an agreement. That's one. Second, I think that the Chamber invited the parties on the 12th of May to agree on the matter, and then to see that - at least I've not read it - but a first proposal to be sent on the 2nd of June is not a sign of great expediency in dealing with the matter. These are two comments on the Chamber receiving it. Of course the Chamber would like to be informed about any progress made in reaching an agreement, but not by reading all the proposals, counter-proposals, et cetera, because that should not be within our sight. When I said they haven't read it, that's true. The -- one of the Legal Officers of the Chamber has read it and told me that in the proposals no attention was paid to when the cross-examining party - and that's what I just talked about - at what point in time the cross-examining party would have to disclose to the party that calls the witness the exhibits it intends to use during cross-examination. The Chamber would like to receive information about results rather than about proposals as soon as possible. Is there any way that we could limit the time -- of course I can't say when to reach an agreement, but of course the Chamber would like to know, well, let's say, one week from now whether substantial progress has been made or whether an agreement has been reached; and if an agreement has been reached, what the agreement is. Because I think as I said before, agreement of the parties is important, but of course the Chamber will also have to accept what the parties agreed upon because it's still the Chamber which is responsible for the conduct of the trial et al. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might ask what form the Chamber would wish to have. If there is agreement, and I expect there will be agreement on a number of matters, what form the Chamber would like that in, in an official filing or simply a letter or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, finally, an official filing would be good, but, as I said before, if you agree. It could be that the Chamber considers that paragraph 7(A) is unsatisfactory for the Chamber. So what I would suggest to the parties that if there is an agreement, that the parties would informally send a copy of the written agreement to the Chamber, the Chamber will then have a look at it, see whether there's any reason to not adopt the whole or part of the agreement. And it's all finalised to have it then officially filed and have it on the record. But I don't think that there is great use in filing the first version at the 1st of September, the second on the 15th of September, the third on the 30th of September, that seems not to be a very practical way of proceeding. So let's, in a rather informal way, inform the Chamber about the results. And once the Chamber has adopted the agreement as a workable one for this trial, then to have everything formally be filed. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court pleases, may we ask the Court for one clarification in this regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours just pointed out to the Prosecution that it's actually bound by its decision on the allocation of hours for witnesses and the number of witnesses, the decision issued by the previous Bench in this case. Now, we have before us a decision on the 6th of May, 2008, rendered by the Chamber in this case on provisions of documents and scheduling of witnesses. And on page 2 the Presiding Judge at that time, Justice Robinson, set out certain criteria for the filing of documents, the number of documents, the time limitations to disclose documents including Prosecution and Defence position. Is it the Court's opinion that this decision is no longer valid in terms of binding the parties? Are the parties therefore at liberty to go beyond or within the limitations the Presiding Judge did set in that order? And if I may just give a short example. The Presiding Judge in that decision introduced a different criteria than in the Perisic case, whereby the number of documents were hundreds, while in this decision the number of pages of hundreds is the criterion for number of hours which should be given to the Prosecution or Defence to disclose it. In other words, is it the Court's opinion that the agreement the parties are able to make can deviate from this previous decision of the 6th of May, 2008?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before in relation to the number of witnesses and the total time for case presentation, I said that decision stands, therefore we expect a new witness list, but we also see that you asked for another witness to be added to that list. And I said if there's any reason why you consider that it should be 133 instead of 130, we'd like to hear from you. These decisions stand but are not carved in stone, which means that if both parties would feel comfortable with a regime which is different, then the mere fact that there is such a decision should not keep you off from informing the Chamber that there is such a decision should not keep you off from informing the Chamber that there is an agreement on a preferred way of proceeding. And as I said before, the Chamber will then consider whether or not we'll adopt or whether we find reasons not to adopt that decision. But I think that decision stands as long, as there's no new one. And from -- what I expect from the parties is to consider that. And if the parties find that there is a better way of proceeding, and a better way which does not in any way -- makes it more difficult for the Chamber to conduct this trial, then of course we'll seriously consider that. Is that an answer to your question, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there -- yes. The finalising of an agreement, the Chamber would really like to receive within a week from now whether any progress has been made and of course preferably what your agreed conclusions were. Any other matter on lists of documents. Then disclosure and translation matters. Are there any matters in this respect which need attention? Mr. Knoops, the Chamber has received a copy of a letter you've sent to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution has indicated in an e-mail to the Defence that it would respond to it. I find some elements in that letter which apparently deal with translation issues. Perhaps it would be a very practical disclosure and translation matters if you would not mind to go through this letter which has not been formally filed, or was it filed? I'm -- no, it's not filed, and it should not be filed because it's correspondence between the parties, but it may be very practical at this moment. First of all, there is the Rule 70 material, Milosevic letter. If you prefer to give your response in writing to Mr. Knoops, fine. If you could inform the Chamber and respond now, we would listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just generally with respect to the entire letter, Your Honour, I met with Mr. Knoops before today's hearing, and all of the matters other than the Rule 70 matter, the Milosevic matter, are resolved. I told him I would be memorialised that in a letter later today, and he should have that. I am prepared to address both Mr. Knoops and the Chamber on the Rule 70 matter. But I would ask that if the Chamber wishes to hear that, that we move into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do then I just briefly mention so that this is on the record that the other matters addressed in this letter were partial disclosure of translations for both Rule 65 ter and Rule 66 material. Mr. Knoops experienced some confusion where translations would be partial translations. That apparently has been resolved. Mr. Knoops very much wished to be informed if any exhibits would be dropped from the Rule 65 ter list or if there were any other changes to the Rule 65 ter list. Apparently that matter has been resolved as well. There was a matter about missing material. Seven documents related to witnesses that would still require translation, and around ten exhibits also waiting for translation. But apparently that matter has been resolved as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so the record is clear, Mr. Knoops has agreed to identify those documents to me today, and we'll make our best efforts to resolve all of them before the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session. My apologies for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you did not do anything wrong, so the apologies are accepted, but at the same time ... The Chamber would like to deliver an oral decision on the ninth and the tenth Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This is the Chamber's decision on the ninth and tenth Prosecution motions for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 29th of April, 2009, the Prosecution filed its ninth Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list seeking leave to add to its exhibit list a notebook which the Prosecutor suspects belongs to Ratko Mladic. On the 7th of May, 2009, the Prosecution filed its tenth Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list seeking leave to add ten additional documents. According to the Prosecution, the documents listed in this motion include a combat report, a military map, and a transcript of intercepted conversation. The Prosecution submits that these documents are highly relevant, providing necessary linkage and crime base evidence. On the 13th of May, 2009, the Simatovic Defence responded to the Prosecution's ninth Rule 65 ter motion, opposing the addition. In support of its objection, it submitted that, considering the present stage of the case, the addition of the notebook would not allow the Defence adequate time and conditions for preparing its defence and stated that the notebook does not meet the requirements of prima facie relevance and probative value. On the 14th of May, 2009, the Stanisic Defence responded to both the ninth and the tenth Rule 65 ter motions. In support of its objection, the Stanisic Defence submitted that the volume and frequency of the proposed additions make the commissioning of new investigations an impossible burden. It also pointed out that the attempt to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list is made at a late stage of proceedings. On the 15th of May, the Prosecution sought leave to reply to the Defence responses. On the 21st of May, the Chamber decided to deny this request and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. The Chamber has discretionary powers to grant a motion to amend the exhibit list if it is satisfied that to do so would be in the interests of justice. In exercising this discretion the Chamber must balance the Prosecution's duty to present the available evidence to prove its case with the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial and the right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of their defence. The Chamber must take into consideration whether the documents sought to be added are prima facie relevant and probative. The Chamber will also consider whether good cause for amending the exhibit list has been shown. Moreover, the Chamber will consider the extent to which the new documents create an additional burden on the Defence. The notebook referred to in the ninth Rule 65 ter motion relates to the accused Stanisic's role in military operations of the Yugoslav Army and the Bosnian Serb army in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 and paramilitary units from Erdut and Djeletovci. The Chamber is satisfied that the notebook is prima facie relevant and of probative value. The various types of documents listed in the tenth Rule 65 ter motion relate to a variety of elements such as the alleged persecution and deportation of non-Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina; the role of the accused or the Serbian Ministry of Interior in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and other related factors. The Chamber also finds that these documents are prima facie relevant and of probative value. The Chamber will further consider the relevance and probative value of the documents and the arguments raised by the Defence when and if the Prosecution tenders these documents into evidence. As for good cause to amend the exhibit list, the Chamber finds that there exists good cause for amending, since the notebook only came into the Prosecution's possession on the 25th of February, 2009. However, the Prosecution in its tenth Rule 65 ter motion failed to provide detailed justification to support the proposed amendment. While the Prosecution provided information on when the documents were or would be disclosed, there are only sporadic indications of when it came into possession of these documents. The Chamber will consider whether it's nevertheless in the interest of justice to grant leave to add these documents to the Prosecution's exhibit list. An important consideration for the Chamber is the extent to which the addition will create an additional burden on the Defence. The documents listed in the tenth Rule 65 ter motion are relatively concise. Most of them only consist of a couple of pages. The volume of the notebook in the ninth Rule 65 ter motion amounts to more than 300 pages. However, the Chamber considers that this trial has not yet commenced and that therefore the Defence has still time to assess all the new documents. In this vein, the Chamber finds that by allowing the Defence reasonable amount of time to review the materials before their actual submission, it is possible to fully accommodate the Defence. In line with the rationale of Rule 65 ter (E)(iii), which provides that the Provence is obliged to present its Rule 65 ter exhibit list to the Defence not later than six weeks before the Pre-Trial Conference, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution should not use the sought material for evidentiary purposes until after six weeks after rendering of the present decision. Or if there are still some pending translations due, after six weeks from receiving such translations by the Defence. Balancing the Prosecution's duty to present the available evidence to prove its case with the right of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial and the right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of the defence, the Trial Chamber concludes that it is in the interests of justice to add the material sought by the Prosecution in its ninth and tenth Rule 65 ter motions to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the ninth and tenth Prosecution motions for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. I have at this moment nothing else on my agenda. Looking at the clock, I establish that this would be the time to have a break after approximately one hour and a half. The last item always is any matter to be raised by the parties. If there is nothing, or if it could be dealt with in one or two minutes, I would like to invite the parties to raise whatever they wish to raise. If, however, it would take more time, then we would first have a break. Mr. Groome, need for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have two matters, Your Honour, that I believe I can take care of in less than a minute. There is just matters to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I would like to hear from the Defence whether there are more matters that take more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No matters. Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, proof of the pudding is in the eating, Mr. Groome, you said two matters of one minute. I'm looking at the clock. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to 92 ter, prior to the start of trial last spring, the Prosecution filed all of its applications for admission of written evidence in lieu of live testimony. At that time we provided the Defence with copies of all the statements or testimony we requested admission of under Rules 92 bis and ter. There was something that Your Honour said at the last Status Conference that made me believe that maybe that wasn't clear for the Chamber, so I just wanted to clarify that. And my remaining 30 seconds, I am happy to report that there has been some progress on agreed facts. Mr. Jovanovic has forwarded an e-mail this morning notifying us of some facts that he will agree to. Obviously an agreed fact has limited utility unless there is agreement between all three parties. To that end, Mr. Knoops has agreed to consider Mr. Jovanovic's e-mail prior to Friday and let us know whether he will also agree to those facts. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome, also for staying within the time-limits. The Chamber will always be delighted if progress is made, but the real moment will be whether the progress has resulted in an agreement. If there's nothing else to be raised at this moment, the Chamber adjourns sine die.
